paras: The lynching threats against John W. Booker were threats made against a sixteen-year-old Black youth after a Democratic political parade in Indianapolis, Indiana, on Saturday night, 22 September 1888. Booker was accused of assaulting a marching member of the Frances Cleveland Club, and an editorial said 'excited Democratic hoodlums' threatened to lynch him. He was not harmed; he was fined in the Mayor's court, and the Republican Indianapolis Journal treated the affair as a partisan overreaction.

The incident took place during a Democratic demonstration in the 1888 presidential campaign; the Journal said the parade also produced a disputed clash between police and visitors from Chicago. The woman involved, Miss Mary K. Miller, belonged to the Frances Cleveland Club of Haughville and was marching in the procession.

According to the Journal's editorial, one of the marching women dropped her handkerchief and a sixteen-year-old 'colored boy' tried to pick it up with a broken cane. She slapped him in the face, and he struck her with the cane, an account Miller herself confirmed in court. The editorial said the assault was 'magnified into a most dastard thing' and that 'threats of lynching' were made in the locality, without further detail. Booker was arrested the same night on a charge of assault and battery with intent to kill.

On Monday morning, 24 September, Miller appeared in court 'apparently unharmed', the charge was reduced to plain assault and battery, and Mayor Denny fined Booker. The next day Booker was arrested again and brought before 'Squire Walpole on a charge of striking Louisa Eckert the same night, but he was released when Eckert testified that he was not the boy who struck her. The Journal reported that 'the colored men of the city are very indignant' at the attempts of 'a few Democrats' to make trouble for him.

The affair was reported in three items in the Republican Indianapolis Journal on 25 and 26 September 1888. Its editorial, 'A Tempest in a Tea-Pot', is the only source for the lynching threats, which it blamed on 'Democratic hoodlums' as part of a broader attack on Democratic conduct during the parade. It called the fine 'utterly disproportionate to the offense', and its court column headed the case 'Was Not Hurt Much' and the rearrest 'A Bit of Democratic Malice'.
The two court reports named the youth differently, as John W. Booker and as Samuel M. Booker, and the fine is given as either $5 and costs or $10.

reader.title: Lynching threats against John W. Booker
bases: The only reported violence against the youth was verbal: an editorial says 'threats of lynching' were made in the locality after the reported assault, and no attack on him is described (A1, A2).

No one was killed or physically attacked; the editorial reports only threats of lynching by 'excited Democratic hoodlums', a group of unstated size, prompted by the reported assault on a club member (A1).
The lynching threats appear only in one Indianapolis Journal editorial (A1); the paper's two court briefs confirm the arrest and fine but do not mention threats (A2, A3).

accounts.label: Indianapolis Journal editorial
accounts.gist: A marching woman dropped her handkerchief, a sixteen-year-old boy tried to pick it up with a broken cane, she slapped him and he hit her; the story was magnified and Democratic hoodlums threatened lynching.

accounts.label: Complainant's testimony (court report)
accounts.gist: Miss Miller said Booker struck her with a small cane after she slapped him; she appeared unharmed and the charge was reduced.

framing.detail: The Republican Indianapolis Journal called the fuss 'A Tempest in a Tea-Pot', blamed 'excited Democratic hoodlums' for the lynching threats and 'Democratic malice' for the rearrest, and said the fine 'should not have been imposed'.

conflicts.note: Same paper on consecutive days; A3 identifies him as the youth fined Monday for striking a young lady in the procession.
The court brief may give the total including costs; neither is clearly better.
